In the bitter cold of Chang'an, snow piled six feet high.
Under the ancient plum tree by the Ba Bridge, the blind musician siblings Dian Xue and Ting Mei played the qin and flute. Lan He, a disciple of the Masked Troupe, passed by and stopped to listen, then took out his Clearwind Xiao to join in harmony. Though not a word was exchanged, their melodies resonated like a shared secret of the heart.
The three drank wine beneath the tree, discussing music until deep into the night. Lan He, flushed with wine, confessed: "After three years of mastering the xiao, my skill has reached its peak, yet I'm often troubled by a single note, pondering it for days—the Clearwind Xiao shapes melodies from the wind, but the wind is the most elusive force in the world. How can one command it?"

Hearing this, Ting Mei, the flutist, untied a cloth pouch from her waist and offered it to him, saying: "Blind since birth, I've grown sensitive to the whispers of the wind, able to 'see' its flow. Unable to describe it to others, I devised this method—burning reed membrane into ash and placing it inside the hollow of the xiao or flute reveals the wind's path."

Lan He tried it and watched as the ash danced with the music: first, the gong note drew the ash into threads; then the shang note scattered it like dust; finally, the jiao and zhi notes made it surge like a spring, blending a thousand sounds.
When the melody ended and the ash settled, Lan He sighed: "A thousand days of practice, and only now do I understand—human music aligns with the rhythms of heaven and earth, and therein lies its essence."

The three spent the night composing "Three Friends of Winter." The pine and bamboo movements came naturally, but the plum blossom movement eluded them. They vowed to meet again and complete it.
At dawn, as the snow cleared, they parted, leaving only echoes in the tree.
